## Setup

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
set.seed(469)
library(vroom)
library(tidyverse)
library(forecast)
library(patchwork)
library(lmtest)
library(prophet)

predictors <- c("Income", "Production", "Savings", "Unemployment")

data <- vroom("C:/Users/aidan/Downloads/CompanyGrowth.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(Qrtr = factor(Qrtr))

data_all <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(PctGrowth), if_all(all_of(predictors), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
  mutate(q  = as.numeric(as.character(Qrtr)),
         ds = as.Date(paste(Year, (q - 1) * 3 + 1, 1, sep = "-")),
         y  = PctGrowth) %>%
  arrange(ds)

tail(data_all)
```

```{r}
# Quarters we need to project (2025 Q3 and Q4)
make_future <- function(train, end_date = as.Date("2025-10-01")) {
  tibble(ds = seq(max(train$ds), end_date, by = "quarter")[-1]) %>%
    mutate(Year = year(ds),
           Qrtr = factor(quarter(ds), levels = levels(train$Qrtr)))
}

future_all <- make_future(data_all)
future_all
```

## Helper functions

```{r}
ts_of <- function(x, df) ts(x, start = c(df$Year[1], df$q[1]), frequency = 4)

metrics <- function(actual, pred) {
  tibble(MAE  = mean(abs(actual - pred)),
         RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2)))
}

# ---- Stage 1: three ways to forecast the four economic indicators ----
forecast_X_lm <- function(train, future) {
  X <- sapply(predictors, function(v)
    predict(lm(as.formula(paste(v, "~ Year + Qrtr")), data = train), newdata = future))
  matrix(X, nrow = nrow(future), dimnames = list(NULL, predictors))
}

forecast_X_arima <- function(train, future) {
  h <- nrow(future)
  X <- sapply(predictors, function(v)
    as.numeric(forecast(auto.arima(ts_of(train[[v]], train), seasonal = TRUE), h = h)$mean))
  matrix(X, nrow = h, dimnames = list(NULL, predictors))
}

fit_prophet <- function(df, regressors = NULL) {
  # yearly.seasonality = 1: quarterly data only supports a low-order seasonal term
  m <- prophet(weekly.seasonality = FALSE, daily.seasonality = FALSE,
               yearly.seasonality = 1, interval.width = 0.95, fit = FALSE)
  for (r in regressors) m <- add_regressor(m, r)
  suppressMessages(fit.prophet(m, df))
}

forecast_X_prophet <- function(train, future) {
  X <- sapply(predictors, function(v) {
    m <- fit_prophet(train %>% transmute(ds, y = .data[[v]]))
    predict(m, future %>% dplyr::select(ds))$yhat
  })
  matrix(X, nrow = nrow(future), dimnames = list(NULL, predictors))
}

# ---- Stage 2: growth models (all use all four predictors) ----
growth_models <- c("MLR", "SARIMA (auto)", "SARIMA (d=0)", "Prophet")

fit_growth <- function(train, model) {
  y_ts <- ts_of(train$PctGrowth, train)
  X_tr <- as.matrix(train[, predictors])
  switch(model,
    "MLR"           = lm(PctGrowth ~ Income + Production + Savings + Unemployment, data = train),
    "SARIMA (auto)" = auto.arima(y_ts, xreg = X_tr, seasonal = TRUE),
    "SARIMA (d=0)"  = auto.arima(y_ts, xreg = X_tr, seasonal = TRUE, d = 0),
    "Prophet"       = fit_prophet(train %>% dplyr::select(ds, y, all_of(predictors)),
                                  regressors = predictors))
}

predict_growth <- function(fit, future, X) {
  if (inherits(fit, "lm")) {
    p <- predict(fit, newdata = as.data.frame(X), interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)
    tibble(Predicted = p[, "fit"], Lower_95 = p[, "lwr"], Upper_95 = p[, "upr"])
  } else if (inherits(fit, "Arima")) {
    fc <- forecast(fit, xreg = X, level = 95)
    tibble(Predicted = as.numeric(fc$mean),
           Lower_95  = as.numeric(fc$lower),
           Upper_95  = as.numeric(fc$upper))
  } else {
    p <- predict(fit, bind_cols(future %>% dplyr::select(ds), as_tibble(X)))
    tibble(Predicted = p$yhat, Lower_95 = p$yhat_lower, Upper_95 = p$yhat_upper)
  }
}

# Which indicator forecast each full pipeline uses for real 2025 projections
own_pipeline <- tribble(
  ~model,          ~X_source,
  "MLR",           "Forecast X: lm trend",
  "SARIMA (auto)", "Forecast X: ARIMA",
  "SARIMA (d=0)",  "Forecast X: ARIMA",
  "Prophet",       "Forecast X: Prophet"
)
```

## Current model: MLR

```{r}
current_model <- lm(PctGrowth ~ Income + Production + Savings + Unemployment, data = data_all)
summary(current_model)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
data_all <- data_all %>%
  mutate(fitted_vals = fitted(current_model),
         resids      = residuals(current_model),
         time        = Year + (q - 1) / 4)

title_theme <- theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10))

p_acf  <- ggAcf(data_all$resids) + labs(title = "ACF of MLR Residuals") + title_theme
p_res  <- ggplot(data_all, aes(fitted_vals, resids)) + geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +

  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "darkgray", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Histogram", x = "Residuals", y = "Count") + title_theme
p_qq   <- ggplot(data_all, aes(sample = resids)) + stat_qq() + stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Normal QQ Plot", x = "Theoretical", y = "Sample") + title_theme
p_time <- ggplot(data_all, aes(time, resids)) + geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals Over Time", x = "Year", y = "Residuals") + title_theme

(p_acf | p_res | p_hist) / (p_qq | p_time)
```

## Holdout test: train through 2024 Q2, test 2024 Q3 – 2025 Q2

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
run_holdout <- function(cut_date) {
  tr <- data_all %>% filter(ds <  cut_date)
  te <- data_all %>% filter(ds >= cut_date)
  label <- paste(format(cut_date), "to 2025 Q2")

  X_sets <- list(
    "Actual X"             = as.matrix(te[, predictors]),
    "Forecast X: lm trend" = forecast_X_lm(tr, te),
    "Forecast X: ARIMA"    = forecast_X_arima(tr, te),
    "Forecast X: Prophet"  = forecast_X_prophet(tr, te)
  )

  fits <- set_names(map(growth_models, ~ fit_growth(tr, .x)), growth_models)

  res <- imap_dfr(fits, function(fit, m) imap_dfr(X_sets, function(X, xs) {
    pred <- predict_growth(fit, te, X)$Predicted
    bind_cols(tibble(test_set = label, n_test = nrow(te), model = m, X_source = xs),
              metrics(te$PctGrowth, pred))
  }))

  base <- bind_cols(tibble(test_set = label, n_test = nrow(te), model = "Mean only", X_source = "-"),
                    metrics(te$PctGrowth, mean(tr$PctGrowth)))

  list(results = bind_rows(res, base), fits = fits, X_sets = X_sets, test = te)
}

hold4 <- run_holdout(as.Date("2024-07-01"))

# Which SARIMA orders were chosen on the training data
hold4$fits[["SARIMA (auto)"]]
hold4$fits[["SARIMA (d=0)"]]
```

```{r}
# Quarter-by-quarter holdout predictions (actual indicators) vs actual growth
holdout_preds <- imap_dfr(hold4$fits, function(fit, m)
  tibble(ds = hold4$test$ds, model = m,
         Predicted = predict_growth(fit, hold4$test, hold4$X_sets[["Actual X"]])$Predicted))

holdout_preds %>%
  mutate(Predicted = round(Predicted, 3)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = Predicted) %>%
  left_join(hold4$test %>% dplyr::select(ds, Actual = PctGrowth), by = "ds")
```

## 2025 projections (all models fit on data through 2025 Q2)

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
final_fits <- set_names(map(growth_models, ~ fit_growth(data_all, .x)), growth_models)

X_future <- list(
  "Forecast X: lm trend" = forecast_X_lm(data_all, future_all),
  "Forecast X: ARIMA"    = forecast_X_arima(data_all, future_all),
  "Forecast X: Prophet"  = forecast_X_prophet(data_all, future_all)
)

# Forecasted indicator values used for 2025 Q3 and Q4 (useful for a slide)
imap_dfr(X_future, ~ as_tibble(.x) %>%
           mutate(X_source = .y, Qrtr = future_all$Qrtr, .before = 1)) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(predictors), ~ round(.x, 3)))

# Final SARIMA model (fit on all data through 2025 Q2)
final_fits[["SARIMA (d=0)"]]
```

```{r}
proj_2025 <- pmap_dfr(own_pipeline, function(model, X_source)
  bind_cols(future_all %>% dplyr::select(Year, Qrtr),
            tibble(Model = model),
            predict_growth(final_fits[[model]], future_all, X_future[[X_source]])))

proj_2025 %>% mutate(across(c(Predicted, Lower_95, Upper_95), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

```{r}
# MLR simulation interval: also includes uncertainty in the forecasted indicators
set.seed(469)
B <- 5000

pred_resids <- sapply(predictors, function(v)
  residuals(lm(as.formula(paste(v, "~ Year + Qrtr")), data = data_all)))
beta          <- coef(final_fits$MLR)
growth_resids <- residuals(final_fits$MLR)
X_lm_future   <- X_future[["Forecast X: lm trend"]]

mlr_sim <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(future_all)), function(i) {
  idx  <- sample(nrow(pred_resids), B, replace = TRUE)
  Xq   <- sweep(pred_resids[idx, predictors], 2, X_lm_future[i, predictors], "+")
  sims <- as.numeric(cbind(1, Xq) %*% beta) + sample(growth_resids, B, replace = TRUE)
  tibble(Year = future_all$Year[i], Qrtr = future_all$Qrtr[i],
         Lower_95_sim = unname(quantile(sims, 0.025)),
         Upper_95_sim = unname(quantile(sims, 0.975)))
})

proj_2025 %>%
  filter(Model == "MLR") %>%
  left_join(mlr_sim, by = c("Year", "Qrtr")) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !Year, ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

## How the indicators relate to growth

```{r}
# Pick the SARIMA version that did better in the holdout
sarima_choice <- "SARIMA (d=0)"   # or "SARIMA (auto)"
sar_fit <- final_fits[[sarima_choice]]

coefficient_table <- bind_rows(
  tibble(predictor = predictors, model = "MLR",
         estimate  = unname(coef(final_fits$MLR)[predictors]),
         se        = unname(sqrt(diag(vcov(final_fits$MLR)))[predictors])),
  tibble(predictor = predictors, model = sarima_choice,
         estimate  = unname(coef(sar_fit)[predictors]),
         se        = unname(sqrt(diag(sar_fit$var.coef))[predictors])),
  prophet::regressor_coefficients(final_fits$Prophet) %>%
    transmute(predictor = regressor, model = "Prophet", estimate = coef, se = NA_real_)
)

coefficient_table %>% mutate(across(c(estimate, se), ~ round(.x, 4)))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| warning: false
relationship_data <- map_dfr(predictors, function(variable) {
  values    <- seq(min(data_all[[variable]]), max(data_all[[variable]]), length.out = 100)
  reference <- median(data_all[[variable]])
    crossing(coefficient_table %>% filter(predictor == variable, model != "Prophet"), value = values) %>%
    mutate(change = estimate * (value - reference),
           margin = 1.96 * se * abs(value - reference),
           lower  = change - margin,
           upper  = change + margin)
})

ggplot(relationship_data, aes(value, change, color = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.15, color = NA, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Predictor Relationships with Company Growth",
       subtitle = "Change relative to each predictor's median (bands = approx. 95% CI where available)",
       x = "Predictor value (original units)", y = "Predicted change in PctGrowth",
       color = "Model", fill = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Choose the model you will present: "MLR", sarima_choice, or "Prophet"
preferred_model <- "SARIMA (d=0)"

variable_labels <- c(
  Income       = "the disposable-income growth indicator",
  Production   = "the US production growth indicator",
  Savings      = "the personal savings change indicator",
  Unemployment = "the unemployment-rate change indicator"
)

board_results <- coefficient_table %>%
  filter(model == preferred_model) %>%
  mutate(
    lower = estimate - 1.96 * se,
    upper = estimate + 1.96 * se,
    significant = !is.na(se) & (lower > 0 | upper < 0),
    effect = paste0("A one-unit increase in ", variable_labels[predictor],
                    " is associated with ", sprintf("%.3f", abs(estimate)),
                    " percentage points ", if_else(estimate >= 0, "higher", "lower"),
                    " predicted quarterly company growth, holding the other predictors fixed"),
    statement = case_when(
      is.na(se)    ~ paste0(effect, " (this model does not report a standard error)."),
      !significant ~ paste0("Changes in ", variable_labels[predictor],
                            " do not have a statistically significant relationship with ",
                            "quarterly company growth in this model, as the confidence interval includes zero."),
      TRUE         ~ paste0(effect, ".")
    )
  )

board_results %>% dplyr::select(predictor, estimate, lower, upper)
cat(paste(board_results$statement, collapse = "\n\n"))
```
# PRESENTATION NOTES FOR MATTHEW

## Slide 1: Current Model (MLR) and 2025 Outlook

**The current method:** We currently use a multiple linear regression (MLR) that predicts each quarter's growth from four economic indicators measured in that same quarter: disposable-income growth, US production growth, personal savings changes, and unemployment-rate changes. It treats every quarter as independent of the ones before it. It explains about 77% of the quarter-to-quarter variation in growth (R² = 0.768).

**How it performs:** We trained the model on data through 2024 Q2 and had it predict the four quarters we hid (2024 Q3 – 2025 Q2).

- Given the actual indicator values for those quarters, its typical error (RMSE) was **0.194 percentage points**.
- When it also had to forecast the indicators, as it must for 2025, the error grew to **0.319**.
- For comparison, simply predicting the historical average every quarter gives an error of 0.358.

**How we got the 2025 projections:** The model needs indicator values for Q3 and Q4 2025, which don't exist yet, so we used two stages:

1. Forecast each indicator for Q3 and Q4 2025 from its long-run trend and typical quarterly pattern (a regression of each indicator on year and quarter).
2. Plug those forecasted indicators into the MLR to get projected growth.

| Quarter | Projected growth | 95% prediction interval | Interval including indicator uncertainty |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q3 2025 | 0.768% | 0.15% to 1.38% | −0.78% to 1.94% |
| Q4 2025 | 0.657% | 0.04% to 1.27% | −0.84% to 1.77% |

The last column comes from a simulation that also accounts for the chance that our indicator forecasts are wrong. It is the more realistic range.

**Concerns with the current model:**

- Its errors are correlated from one quarter to the next (Ljung-Box p = 0.029), which breaks its independence assumption.
- Its errors are not normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.001).
- Their spread is uneven (Breusch-Pagan p = 0.024).

As a result, its standard intervals are probably too narrow.

## Slide 2: Two Alternative Models

Both alternatives use the same four indicators as the current model. The difference is that they also learn from the company's own recent history.

**1. SARIMA (regression with ARIMA errors)** has two parts:

$$\text{Growth}_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{Income}_t + \beta_2\,\text{Production}_t + \beta_3\,\text{Savings}_t + \beta_4\,\text{Unemployment}_t + \eta_t$$

$$\eta_t = \phi\,\eta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t + \theta\,\varepsilon_{t-1}$$

Fitted on all data through 2025 Q2:

$$\text{Growth}_t = 0.239 + 0.761\,\text{Income}_t + 0.049\,\text{Production}_t - 0.054\,\text{Savings}_t - 0.147\,\text{Unemployment}_t + \eta_t$$

$$\eta_t = -0.756\,\eta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t + 0.643\,\varepsilon_{t-1}, \qquad \sigma^2 = 0.095$$

- The first line is the same regression we use today.
- The second line models the "surprise," the part of growth the economy doesn't explain. Instead of assuming each quarter's surprise is independent, it lets this quarter's surprise depend on last quarter's.
- In our data, the two error terms have opposite signs and largely offset each other. The net effect is a mild give-back: when growth beats what the economy predicted, part of that excess tends to reverse the next quarter.
- The automatic selection procedure first chose a version that modeled quarter-to-quarter *changes* in growth. That version showed a classic sign of being over-adjusted (a moving-average term of −0.98, almost exactly cancelling the change) and left correlated errors. Growth is already a rate of change with no long-run drift, so we fit growth directly. The final model uses ARIMA(1,0,1) errors.
- Seasonal (quarterly) terms were considered and not selected.

**2. Prophet** is a forecasting model developed by Meta. It breaks growth into a smooth baseline trend that can shift over time, a repeating within-year pattern, and the effects of the four indicators. It is more flexible than MLR or SARIMA, but also more complex and harder to interpret.

**How we got their 2025 projections:** The same two-stage approach as Slide 1, except that each model forecasts the indicators its own way. SARIMA uses an automatically selected time-series model for each indicator, and Prophet uses a separate Prophet model for each indicator.

## Slide 3: Model Comparison and Recommendation

**Testing method:** Every model was trained on data through 2024 Q2 and asked to predict 2024 Q3 – 2025 Q2, which were hidden from it. We ran this two ways:

- **Actual indicators:** each model was given the real indicator values for those quarters. This isolates how good each growth model is.
- **Forecasted indicators:** each model first had to forecast the indicators, just as it will for 2025. This shows realistic forecast accuracy.

We measured accuracy with RMSE, the typical prediction error in percentage points (lower is better). As a check, we repeated the test using only the last three quarters.

| Model | Actual indicators (4 qtrs) | Actual indicators (3 qtrs) | Forecasted indicators (4 qtrs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prophet | **0.177** | **0.204** | 0.329 |
| SARIMA | 0.186 | 0.206 | 0.361 |
| MLR (current) | 0.194 | 0.214 | **0.319** |
| Historical average only | 0.358 | 0.408 | 0.358 |

**What the results show:**

- **With actual indicators, both alternatives beat the current model.** Prophet was slightly most accurate, followed by SARIMA. The three-quarter check gave the same ranking.
- **All models missed the first half of 2025 in the same direction.** They predicted about 0.5% for Q1 (actual: 0.28%) and 0.84–0.92% for Q2 (actual: 1.11%).
- **With forecasted indicators, errors rose to 0.32–0.36 for every model**, close to simply predicting the average. The biggest source of error is predicting the economy, not the choice of growth model. When given the *same* indicator forecasts, SARIMA and MLR scored almost identically (0.318 vs. 0.319).
- **The differences between models are small** and based on only four quarters, so they should be read as modest, not decisive.

**2025 projections compared (95% intervals in parentheses):**

| Quarter | MLR (current) | SARIMA | Prophet |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q3 2025 | 0.77% (0.15, 1.38) | 0.63% (0.02, 1.23) | 0.64% (0.05, 1.21) |
| Q4 2025 | 0.66% (0.04, 1.27) | 0.77% (0.17, 1.38) | 0.56% (−0.02, 1.14) |

- **All three project positive growth of roughly 0.55–0.8% per quarter, and their intervals overlap almost completely.**
- **Part of their disagreement comes from different indicator forecasts.** For example, the Q3 savings forecast ranges from −2.1 to +3.3 depending on the method.
- **These intervals assume the indicator forecasts are correct.** Slide 1's simulation suggests the real uncertainty is closer to ±1.3 percentage points.

**Recommendation: move from MLR to SARIMA.**

1. **More accurate than the current model:** 0.186 vs. 0.194, and 0.206 vs. 0.214 on the three-quarter check.
2. **Statistically sound.** It is the only model whose errors pass the test for leftover correlation between quarters (Ljung-Box p = 0.064, vs. 0.029 for MLR and 0.010 for Prophet), so its confidence and prediction intervals are more trustworthy.
3. **Simple and interpretable.** It is the regression the board already knows plus one correction term for last quarter's surprise, and it gives clear indicator effects with confidence intervals (Slide 4).

**Why not Prophet?** Prophet had the lowest error, but its edge over SARIMA is small: about 0.01 points on four quarters and 0.002 on three, so one quarter could flip the ranking. In exchange, it is more complex, leaves correlated errors, and does not provide confidence intervals for the indicator effects the board asked about. We judged that a small, uncertain accuracy gain wasn't worth those costs.

**One caveat:** switching models will not fix the larger challenge. Our 2025 forecasts are only as good as our forecasts of the economy.

## Slide 4: How the Economic Indicators Relate to Growth (SARIMA)

Holding the other indicators constant:

- **Disposable income:** a one-unit increase is associated with **0.761 percentage points higher** quarterly growth (95% CI: 0.685 to 0.837). This is by far the strongest driver, consistent with VistaLux selling discretionary, high-end products.
- **US production:** a one-unit increase is associated with **0.049 percentage points higher** growth (95% CI: 0.006 to 0.092). This is a small but real positive effect.
- **Personal savings:** a one-unit increase is associated with **0.054 percentage points lower** growth (95% CI: −0.0598 to −0.0485). When households save more, they spend less on optional purchases. Because this indicator swings widely (roughly −60 to +40), a 10-unit rise corresponds to about 0.5 points lower growth.
- **Unemployment:** changes in the unemployment rate do **not** have a statistically significant relationship with growth once the other three are accounted for (95% CI: −0.328 to 0.034).

The current MLR model gives nearly identical estimates, so these conclusions hold regardless of which model is used. SARIMA's intervals are more trustworthy because they account for the quarter-to-quarter correlation that MLR ignores.

**Limitations:**

- Prediction errors are heavier-tailed than a normal distribution, so stated intervals are approximate.
- The model comparison rests on only four test quarters.
- The 2025 projections depend heavily on forecasts of the economic indicators. The SARIMA and Prophet intervals shown do not include that extra uncertainty.
- All three models show a leftover dip in residual correlation at lag 7 (quarters about seven apart), which none of them captures; it is unlikely to affect two-quarter-ahead forecasts.
